analysis.one_liner: Bans airlines from charging fees that exceed their actual costs for changes, cancellations, and baggage.
analysis.headline: The bill to stop airlines from charging fees far above their real costs never got a vote in the House committee it was sent to.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR Fees Act would have required the Department of Transportation to write rules barring airlines from charging fees that are unreasonable or out of proportion to what the fee actually costs the airline. It covers change and cancellation fees, checked baggage fees, and any other flight-related fee. Airlines would have to show the fee matches real costs like electronic processing and labor. The bill never moved after being referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers, who currently pay change fees of up to $200, cancellation fees, and checked bag fees that often bear little relation to the airline's actual cost of handling the bag or processing the change. The bill would force those fees down to something close to cost.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers paying bag and change fees

how_it_helps.text: Within 270 days of passage, the Transportation Department would have to write regulations prohibiting fees on flight changes, cancellations, checked bags, and other flight-related charges that are 'unreasonable or disproportional to the costs incurred' [S2][S3].

The bill spells out what counts as a real cost: for change and cancellation fees, the airline's ability to resell the seat, the fare a replacement passenger would pay, and electronic processing and labor costs; for bag fees, the actual cost of handling baggage [S3].
The Transportation Department would have to update the standards at least every three years, so the fee limits could not go stale [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which collected tens of billions of dollars in baggage and change fees over the past decade. Fees that cannot be justified by actual costs would have to shrink or disappear, cutting a major revenue stream that does not show up in the advertised ticket price.

drawbacks.text: Defining 'reasonable and proportional' through federal regulation is inherently imprecise. The bill leaves the details to the Transportation Department, and a rule-writing process could be slow, contested, or tailored by whichever administration holds office at the time [S3].
If change and cancellation fees fall, airlines may respond by raising base fares for everyone, so passengers who never change their tickets could end up paying part of the cost.

Airlines argue that fee-for-service pricing lets infrequent or no-frills travelers pay less, and that blanket cost-based limits remove flexibility to offer different service levels at different prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to travelers is direct and easy to see: fees that cost the airline almost nothing to process, like a $200 change fee or a bag fee well above handling cost, would have to come down. The main cost is uncertainty — airlines could recoup some revenue through higher base fares, and the rule's definition of 'proportional' would be fought over in the regulatory process. On balance, the bill targeted a pricing practice that travelers cannot avoid once they have bought a ticket, and the potential savings for frequent flyers and families checking bags are substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then to its Aviation Subcommittee, and sat there until the two-year Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on November 20, 2019, with 11 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the same day, and the next day to the Aviation Subcommittee [S1][S5].
Seventeen House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no committee vote, no House floor debate, and no Senate companion action; the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines are better off, because the fee revenue the bill targeted — checked bag and change fees that can far exceed the airline's actual cost — stayed untouched. Travelers kept paying the fees as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, whose fee revenue stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Fees Act to force airline fees down to actual cost.

for.name: 17 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Peter DeFazio (D)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral — no markup, no committee vote, no report to the floor in the 14 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. airline industry
against.role: Carriers collecting baggage and change fees
against.what_they_did: Airline carriers have long opposed cost-based limits on ancillary fees, which are among their most profitable revenue streams, and the bill died without ever reaching a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-controlled committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: Baggage and change fees are a multi-billion-dollar revenue stream that often exceeds the airline's actual cost of handling the bag or processing the change, and they are not included in advertised fares. The bill would cap those fees at roughly cost, directly cutting airline revenue in a way that lowers prices for travelers.
